title: Linux Essentials
tagline: LPI Linux Essentials & LF essentials concepts
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by LPI or the Linux Foundation. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: Picking a distro for a library kiosk
scenarios.situation: A small library needs 20 public kiosks that must run untouched for five years with security patches but no surprise interface changes. Two volunteers propose different distros: one a rolling release, one a long-term-support (LTS) release.
scenarios.prompt: Which choice fits the requirement, and why?
choices: The LTS release — fixed versions with years of security updates and no forced feature changes
The rolling release — newest packages mean fewer patches to apply over time
Either is fine — kiosks don't need updates once deployed
The rolling release — LTS releases stop getting security patches after one year
scenarios.why: LTS releases freeze the software versions and backport security fixes for many years, giving stability and predictability — exactly what unattended kiosks need. Rolling releases change continuously, which risks breaking a locked-down kiosk setup.
scenarios.hint: What does 'long-term support' promise about change over time?

scenarios.title: The modified GPL tool
scenarios.situation: Your team takes an open-source backup tool licensed under GPLv2, modifies it for internal use, and now wants to sell the modified version to customers as a closed product.
scenarios.prompt: What does the GPL require here?
choices: If you distribute the modified program, you must make its source code available under the GPL as well
You can sell it closed-source as long as you credit the original authors in the README
The GPL only applies to non-commercial use, so selling is unrestricted
You must pay the original authors a licensing fee before distributing
scenarios.why: The GPL is a copyleft license: anyone who distributes a modified version must license the whole work under the GPL and provide source. Selling is allowed, but keeping the modifications closed is not. Permissive licenses like MIT or Apache-2.0 would allow closed distribution.
scenarios.hint: What makes a license 'copyleft' rather than permissive?

scenarios.title: Free as in freedom
scenarios.situation: A vendor advertises its product as 'free software' but ships only binaries, forbids reverse engineering, and offers no source code.
scenarios.prompt: Under the Free Software Foundation's definition, is this free software?
choices: No — the four freedoms require the freedom to run, study, share, and modify, which needs source access
Yes — 'free' refers to the price being zero, which the vendor satisfies
Yes — binaries count as long as the vendor provides documentation
No — but only because the vendor charges for support contracts
scenarios.why: The FSF defines free software by four freedoms: to run, study (requires source), redistribute, and modify/improve (requires source). Zero price is 'gratis'; freedom is 'libre'. Without source, freedoms 1 and 3 are impossible, so it is not free software by this definition.
scenarios.hint: Which of the four freedoms is impossible without source code?

scenarios.title: The unanswered forum post
scenarios.situation: You post 'My WiFi doesn't work, please help ASAP!!!' to a distro forum and get no replies. A moderator later answers a different post that included the distro version, the exact error from dmesg, and the commands already tried.
scenarios.prompt: What should your next post include to get help?
choices: Distro and kernel version, the exact error output, hardware details, and what you already tried
A demand for faster support, since forums are obligated to answer
Your root password so helpers can SSH in and fix it
The same message reposted every hour until someone responds
scenarios.why: Community support runs on good bug reports: version info (lsb_release -a, uname -r), exact error text, relevant logs (dmesg, journalctl), and steps already attempted. Volunteers can't diagnose 'doesn't work'. Demanding help or sharing credentials violates community norms and basic security.
scenarios.hint: What information would YOU need to diagnose someone else's WiFi?

scenarios.title: Two passwd pages
scenarios.situation: You run 'man passwd' to change your password and get a page about the /etc/passwd file format instead of the command. A colleague says to check the manual section numbers.
scenarios.prompt: Which command shows the password-changing command's page, and what do the sections mean?
choices: man 1 passwd — section 1 is user commands, section 5 is file formats
man 5 passwd — section 5 overrides section 1 for commands
man -a passwd — the -a flag deletes the wrong page
info passwd — man pages never cover the passwd command
scenarios.why: Man pages are organized in sections: 1 = user commands, 5 = file formats and conventions, 8 = system administration. Both a command and a file named passwd exist, so 'man 1 passwd' selects the command explicitly. 'man -a' would show all matching pages in sequence.
scenarios.hint: Which section number is associated with ordinary commands you type?

scenarios.title: Junior admin or cloud engineer?
scenarios.situation: Two entry-level postings: (A) 'Junior Linux Administrator — on-prem servers, patching, user accounts, backups' and (B) 'Junior Cloud Engineer — Terraform, CI/CD pipelines, Kubernetes'. You have Linux Essentials-level skills plus basic shell scripting.
scenarios.prompt: Which role is the more realistic next step, and what bridges the gap to the other?
choices: Role A fits now — Linux fundamentals map directly to admin work; scripting plus IaC/Kubernetes study bridges to role B
Role B fits now — cloud titles don't require Linux knowledge
Neither — you must earn a senior certification before applying to any IT job
Role A fits now — and role B will never require Linux skills
scenarios.why: Junior admin work is the direct application of Linux Essentials skills (users, permissions, services, patching). Cloud engineering builds on that same foundation plus automation (IaC, containers, CI/CD) — a learnable bridge, not a different universe. Cloud roles absolutely require Linux fluency.
scenarios.hint: Which posting lists tasks you could already do today?

scenarios.title: Lost in the filesystem
scenarios.situation: You're in /home/ana/projects and need to reach /home/ana/docs. You type 'cd home/ana/docs' and get 'No such file or directory'.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong, and what are two correct ways to get there?
choices: Without a leading /, the path is relative to the current directory — use 'cd /home/ana/docs' or 'cd ../docs'
cd can't move between directories — use the file manager
You must use 'cd home/ana/docs/' with a trailing slash
The docs directory doesn't exist — relative paths create it automatically
scenarios.why: Paths starting with / are absolute (from root); anything else is relative to the current working directory, so 'home/ana/docs' meant /home/ana/projects/home/ana/docs. '..' means the parent directory, so '../docs' goes up one then into docs. 'pwd' shows where you are; 'cd -' jumps back to the previous directory.
scenarios.hint: What directory did the shell look inside when you typed that?

scenarios.title: Reading ls -l
scenarios.situation: A directory listing shows: 'drwxr-xr-x', '-rw-r--r--', and 'lrwxrwxrwx'. A teammate asks which entries are directories, regular files, and links.
scenarios.prompt: How do you tell from the first character?
evidence:
drwxr-xr-x  4 ana ana 4096 Oct  3 09:12 projects
-rw-r--r--  1 ana ana  220 Oct  3 09:12 notes.txt
lrwxrwxrwx  1 ana ana    8 Oct  3 09:12 latest -> notes.txt
choices: d = directory, - = regular file, l = symbolic link (the '->' shows its target)
d = deleted, - = normal, l = locked
The first character is random padding — use the file command instead
d = disk, - = network file, l = local file
scenarios.why: The first character of ls -l output is the file type: d directory, - regular file, l symlink, plus c/b device files, p pipes, s sockets. The 'latest -> notes.txt' arrow confirms the symlink's target. 'ls -la' also shows hidden dotfiles.
scenarios.hint: What single character differs at the start of each line?

scenarios.title: Where do the logs live?
scenarios.situation: An application writes logs, configs, and user uploads. The team argues about where each belongs: /etc, /var, /home, /opt, /srv.
scenarios.prompt: Match each data type to its FHS home.
choices: Configs → /etc, logs and spools → /var, user files → /home, served data → /srv, third-party apps → /opt
Everything → /home — the FHS is just a suggestion nobody follows
Configs → /var, logs → /etc, user files → /opt
Logs → /tmp so they're cleaned automatically, configs → /home
scenarios.why: The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: /etc holds host-specific config, /var holds variable data (logs, mail spools, caches), /home holds user files, /srv holds data served by the system, /opt holds optional third-party software. Putting logs in /tmp risks losing them on reboot and filling a small tmpfs.
scenarios.hint: Which directory's name hints at 'variable' data that changes constantly?

scenarios.title: Which python am I running?
scenarios.situation: 'python3 --version' says 3.12 but your project expects 3.11. You suspect there are multiple python3 binaries and the wrong one is first in PATH.
scenarios.prompt: How do you investigate?
choices: 'which -a python3' or 'type -a python3' lists every match in PATH order, showing which one wins
'find / -name python3' — the only reliable way
Reinstall python3 — duplicates are always a broken install
Check /etc/passwd — it records the default python
scenarios.why: The shell resolves commands by scanning PATH left to right; 'which -a'/'type -a' shows all matches in that order so you can see shadowing. 'whereis' also shows binary, source, and man locations. find / works but is slow and shows files PATH would never execute.
scenarios.hint: How does the shell decide which python3 runs when several exist?

scenarios.title: The 400-character command
scenarios.situation: You need to rerun a long rsync command from yesterday with one path changed. Retyping it would take minutes and invite typos.
scenarios.prompt: What are the fastest shell-native ways to recall and edit it?
choices: Ctrl+R to reverse-search history, or 'history | grep rsync' then '!n' — then edit on the command line with tab completion
Scroll up with the mouse — terminals keep infinite scrollback
Commands can't be recalled — rewrite it from memory
history shows commands but they can't be edited or rerun
scenarios.why: Ctrl+R incrementally searches history as you type; '!n' re-executes history entry n; '!!' repeats the last command; tab completes paths. Recalled commands land on the editable command line, so you change the one path and hit Enter — fast and typo-resistant.
scenarios.hint: What key combo searches your command history as you type?

scenarios.title: Where is the config?
scenarios.situation: An app's docs say its config is in '~/.config/myapp/', but 'ls ~/.config' shows nothing. 'ls -la ~/.config' shows the myapp directory.
scenarios.prompt: Why the difference?
choices: Files and directories starting with '.' are hidden — plain 'ls' skips them; 'ls -a' shows them
The directory was deleted between the two commands
~/.config is a symlink that only -a can follow
ls caches results — the second listing was stale
scenarios.why: Dotfiles (names starting with .) are hidden by convention — the shell and ls skip them unless asked (-a/--all). User configs live in dotfiles/directories under $HOME (~/.bashrc, ~/.config, ~/.ssh) precisely to stay out of the way. '~' expands to your home directory.
scenarios.hint: What is special about names that begin with a dot?

scenarios.title: Where did the errors go?
scenarios.situation: You run 'find / -name secret.txt > results.txt' and the terminal still floods with 'Permission denied' messages, while results.txt looks incomplete.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and how do you capture both streams properly?
choices: > captures only stdout — errors go to stderr; use 'find / -name secret.txt > results.txt 2> errors.txt' or '2>&1' to combine
> captures everything — the flood means the redirect failed
Use >> instead of > — single > drops stderr
Errors can't be redirected — only stdout can
scenarios.why: Every process has two output streams: stdout (fd 1, the results) and stderr (fd 2, the errors). '>' redirects only stdout. '2>' redirects stderr separately; '2>&1' merges stderr into stdout ('> file 2>&1'); '&>' does both in bash. The Permission denied noise was stderr all along.
scenarios.hint: How many output streams does a process have, and which one did > capture?

scenarios.title: Chaining the pipeline
scenarios.situation: You need the 5 largest .log files under /var/log, showing only filename and size, sorted biggest first.
scenarios.prompt: Which pipeline does it?
choices: find /var/log -name '*.log' -exec ls -lh {} + | sort -k5 -hr | head -5
ls -lh /var/log/*.log | sort | tail -5
find /var/log > sort > head -5
cat /var/log/*.log | sort -n | head
scenarios.why: Pipes (|) feed one command's stdout into the next's stdin. find locates the files, ls -lh gives human sizes, sort -k5 -hr sorts by the size column human-numerically in reverse, head -5 takes the top. Note: plain 'ls /var/log/*.log' misses subdirectories — find recurses. Each stage does one job (Unix philosophy).
scenarios.hint: Which command finds files recursively, and how do you sort by size descending?

scenarios.title: Build, test, deploy — conditionally
scenarios.situation: You want: compile the code; ONLY if compilation succeeds, run tests; then ALWAYS print 'done' at the end.
scenarios.prompt: Which chaining expresses this?
choices: make && make test; echo done — && runs the next only on success, ; always runs
make; make test; echo done — ; already means 'only on success'
make || make test; echo done — || is the success operator
make && make test && echo done — echo must also be conditional
scenarios.why: && chains on success (exit 0), || chains on failure (non-zero), and ; sequences unconditionally. 'make && make test' skips tests if the build fails; '; echo done' runs regardless. Exit codes are the whole mechanism — 'echo $?' inspects the last one.
scenarios.hint: Which operator means 'only if the previous succeeded'?

scenarios.title: The rm that matched too much
scenarios.situation: You meant to delete backup files 'rm *.bak' but the directory also contained 'important.bakcup' — safe. Then you tried 'rm * .bak' (with a space) and chaos ensued.
scenarios.prompt: What did the shell actually expand, and what's the lesson?
choices: '*' matched every file and '.bak' matched nothing extra — the shell expands globs BEFORE rm runs, so rm saw the full file list; always echo the glob first
rm interprets * itself — the shell passes it literally
The space made rm delete only .bak — spaces are safe
Globs only match hidden files — visible files were safe
scenarios.why: Glob expansion happens in the shell before the command executes: 'rm * .bak' became 'rm <every file> .bak'. The command never sees the '*'. Safety habits: 'echo *.bak' to preview, use 'ls' first, quote patterns when passing them to tools like find/grep that do their own matching ('find . -name "*.bak"').
scenarios.hint: Who expands the * — rm, or the shell before rm starts?

scenarios.title: First sudo on a fresh VM
scenarios.situation: On a fresh Debian VM, your user runs 'sudo apt update' and gets 'user is not in the sudoers file'. On your RHEL box the same user works fine.
scenarios.prompt: What differs, and what's the proper fix?
choices: Debian doesn't add the first user to sudo by default (RHEL adds to wheel) — as root, run 'usermod -aG sudo <user>' (or edit sudoers via visudo)
sudo is broken on Debian — reinstall the OS
The user needs the root password, not sudo
sudoers files can't be edited — the VM is unusable
scenarios.why: sudo consults /etc/sudoers (and /etc/sudoers.d/): Debian grants sudo to the 'sudo' group, RHEL-family to 'wheel'. Adding the user to the right group with 'usermod -aG' is the standard fix (re-login needed). Always edit sudoers with visudo — it syntax-checks, since a broken sudoers locks out all sudo.
scenarios.hint: Which group name grants sudo on Debian vs RHEL?

scenarios.title: The script that works for you only
scenarios.situation: Your deploy script uses a tool in ~/bin. It works when you run it, but fails for a teammate with 'command not found' — and fails in cron for you too.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and the robust fix?
choices: ~/bin is on YOUR interactive PATH but not theirs (or cron's minimal PATH) — use absolute paths or set/export PATH inside the script
Scripts can't use tools from ~/bin — move the tool to /usr/bin
cron doesn't run scripts — use systemd timers instead
The teammate needs your password to access ~/bin
scenarios.why: PATH is per-process: your interactive shell may include ~/bin via .bashrc, but teammates and cron have different (cron's is minimal: /usr/bin:/bin). Robust scripts don't depend on ambient PATH — either use absolute paths or set PATH explicitly at the top. 'export' makes a variable visible to child processes.
scenarios.hint: Whose PATH does a cron job inherit?

scenarios.title: Decoding 754
scenarios.situation: A script must be: fully usable by its owner, readable/executable by the group, readable-only by others. A teammate suggests 'chmod 754' but can't explain it.
scenarios.prompt: Is 754 correct, and how does octal map to rwx?
choices: Yes — 7=rwx (owner), 5=r-x (group), 4=r-- (others); each digit sums r=4, w=2, x=1
No — 754 gives the group write access
Octal is deprecated — only symbolic modes work now
754 means something different for scripts vs data files
scenarios.why: Each octal digit = one permission triple, summing read(4)+write(2)+execute(1): 7=4+2+1 (rwx), 5=4+1 (r-x), 4=4 (r--). So 754 = rwxr-xr--. Common defaults: 755 for executables/directories, 644 for data files, 600 for private files. Symbolic equivalent: 'chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o=r'.
scenarios.hint: What do 4, 2, and 1 stand for?

scenarios.title: Wrong owner after the restore
scenarios.situation: After restoring /srv/www from backup, all files are owned by root:root. The web server runs as www-data and needs to read them; developers in group 'webdev' need write access.
scenarios.prompt: What ownership and permission setup fits?
choices: chown -R root:webdev /srv/www with 755/644 (or 775/664 if group writes), ensuring www-data can read via other or group
chown -R www-data:www-data — developers should edit as www-data
chmod -R 777 — simplest and always works
Ownership doesn't matter — only permissions do
scenarios.why: chown sets user:group; the web server typically needs only read (other r-x/r-- suffices, or add www-data to webdev). 777 is never the answer — it's a security hole. Only root can change file ownership (chown), while owners can change group to groups they belong to (chgrp). Recursive -R applies to the tree.
scenarios.hint: Who needs which access — read, write, or both?

scenarios.title: New files are too open
scenarios.situation: New files you create are 664 and new directories 775, but the security policy wants 640/750. Your umask is 002.
scenarios.prompt: What umask gives the desired defaults, and how is it computed?
choices: umask 027 — subtract from 666 (files) and 777 (dirs): 666-027=640, 777-027=750
umask 640 — the umask equals the desired permission
umask 000 — least mask gives most restrictive files
chmod the umask file in /etc — umask can't be changed per session
scenarios.why: umask masks OUT permission bits from the defaults (666 files, 777 dirs): subtract (bitwise) the mask. 027 removes write-for-group? No: 027 = remove all for other (7) + write for group (2): files 666→640, dirs 777→750. Common values: 022 (755/644), 027 (750/640), 077 (700/600). Set it in ~/.bashrc or /etc/profile for persistence.
scenarios.hint: Does umask add permissions or remove them?

scenarios.title: The shared /tmp mystery
scenarios.situation: 'ls -ld /tmp' shows 'drwxrwxrwt'. A user asks why everyone can write there but can't delete each other's files.
scenarios.prompt: What does the 't' mean?
choices: The sticky bit — anyone can create files, but only the owner (or root) can delete/rename them
t means 'temporary' — the kernel wipes it hourly
It's a typo — permissions can't end in t
t means the directory is encrypted
scenarios.why: The sticky bit (1 in the leading octal digit, shown as t on the execute bit) on a world-writable directory restricts deletion to file owners. /tmp is classically 1777. Related special bits: setuid (4, run as file owner — e.g., passwd), setgid (2, run as group owner / inherit group on directories). Shown as s/S when the execute bit is set/unset.
scenarios.hint: Who can delete a file in a sticky-bit directory?

scenarios.title: Link or copy?
scenarios.situation: You need /opt/app/config.yaml also visible at /etc/app/config.yaml, always in sync. A hard link works — until someone moves /opt to another filesystem.
scenarios.prompt: Hard link vs symlink — what breaks, and what's the right call?
choices: Use a symlink — hard links can't cross filesystems and break confusingly; symlinks store a path and work across filesystems (but dangle if the target moves)
Hard links are always better — they never break
Copy the file with cron — links are unreliable
Symlinks can't point to files — only directories
scenarios.why: Hard links are additional directory entries pointing at the same inode: same filesystem only, no directories, deleting one name doesn't delete data. Symlinks are tiny files containing a path: cross filesystems, can point anywhere, but dangle if the target moves/deletes. For config visibility across the system, symlinks are the standard choice.
scenarios.hint: What does each link type actually store — an inode reference or a path?

scenarios.title: Unpacking the release tarball
scenarios.situation: You download app-2.0.tar.gz. You need to list its contents without extracting, then extract it into /opt.
scenarios.prompt: Which tar invocations do this?
choices: tar -tzvf app-2.0.tar.gz (list) then tar -xzvf app-2.0.tar.gz -C /opt (extract)
tar -xvf app-2.0.tar.gz --list then mv
gzip -d then tar -xf — tar can't handle .gz directly
unzip app-2.0.tar.gz — tar and zip are the same
scenarios.why: tar flags: c create, x extract, t list, v verbose, f file, z gzip, j bzip2, J xz, -C change directory. Modern tar auto-detects compression, so -xvf often suffices, but explicit -z is clear. Always list (-t) before extracting untrusted tarballs — they may not contain a top-level directory and can scatter files ('tarbomb').
scenarios.hint: Which single letter switches between create, extract, and list?

scenarios.title: The process that won't die
scenarios.situation: An app hangs. 'kill <pid>' does nothing. A teammate says 'just use kill -9' for everything.
scenarios.prompt: What is the disciplined escalation, and why not start with -9?
choices: kill (SIGTERM, 15) first — lets the process clean up; escalate to kill -9 (SIGKILL) only if TERM is ignored, since KILL can't be caught and may corrupt state
Always start with kill -9 — it's faster
kill -9 is gentle — the numbers are reversed
Reboot — processes can't be killed individually
scenarios.why: SIGTERM (default) asks the process to terminate gracefully — flush buffers, close connections, remove lock files. SIGKILL (-9) is uncatchable and immediate: no cleanup, risking corrupt files and orphaned locks. Escalation ladder: TERM → wait → KILL. pkill/killall target by name; 'ps aux' or 'pgrep' finds PIDs.
scenarios.hint: Which signal can a process catch and handle, and which can it not?

scenarios.title: The forgotten background job
scenarios.situation: You start a long backup in the terminal, then realize you need the prompt back. Ctrl+C would kill it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you background it without losing it?
choices: Ctrl+Z to suspend, then 'bg' to resume in background; 'jobs' lists them, 'fg' brings one back
Ctrl+C then restart with & — the only way
Close the terminal — jobs survive automatically
Jobs can't be backgrounded after starting
scenarios.why: Job control: Ctrl+Z suspends the foreground job, 'bg' resumes it in the background, 'fg %n' brings job n forward, 'jobs' lists them. Better yet, start long jobs with '&' (or use nohup/tmux/screen so they survive terminal closure — plain background jobs die with SIGHUP when the shell exits).
scenarios.hint: What suspends a job, and what resumes it in the background?

scenarios.title: Finding the error lines
scenarios.situation: A 2 GB log file needs: lines containing 'ERROR' (any case), excluding health-check noise, showing line numbers.
scenarios.prompt: Which grep invocation does this?
choices: grep -in 'ERROR' app.log | grep -v 'healthcheck'
grep 'ERROR' app.log — case and noise don't matter
cat app.log | grep ERROR — cat is required for grep
grep -v 'ERROR' — -v selects matching lines
scenarios.why: -i case-insensitive, -n line numbers, -v inverts (excludes). Piping to a second grep -v filters noise. Regex basics extend this: '^ERROR' (line start), 'error.*timeout' (pattern), -E for extended regex (alternation with |). 'grep -r' recurses directories; --include='*.log' narrows it.
scenarios.hint: Which flags ignore case, number lines, and invert the match?

scenarios.title: Top 10 IPs in the access log
scenarios.situation: From an Apache access log, you need the 10 most frequent client IPs with counts, sorted descending.
scenarios.prompt: Which pipeline does it?
choices: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -10
sort access.log | head -10 — IPs sort themselves
uniq -c access.log | sort — uniq counts without sorting first
grep -c IP access.log — counts all at once
scenarios.why: The classic text pipeline: awk extracts field 1 (the IP), sort groups identical lines (required — uniq only collapses ADJACENT duplicates), uniq -c counts, sort -rn sorts numerically descending, head takes 10. Each tool does one thing; the pipe composes them. Variations: cut -d' ' -f1 instead of awk.
scenarios.hint: Why must sort come before uniq -c?

scenarios.title: Cleaning old temp files
scenarios.situation: You must find files under /var/tmp older than 30 days and delete them — but preview the list first.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe find workflow?
choices: find /var/tmp -type f -mtime +30 -print (preview), then replace -print with -delete (or -exec rm {} +)
find /var/tmp -mtime 30 -exec rm -rf {} \; — run it directly
ls -lt /var/tmp | head — simpler and equivalent
rm /var/tmp/* — temp files are always safe to delete
scenarios.why: find predicates: -type f (files only), -mtime +30 (modified more than 30 days ago — '+' means greater than). Always -print first to preview; then -delete (efficient, no fork) or -exec rm {} +. Never rm -rf a tmp dir blindly — other processes may hold files open, and a typo'd path is catastrophic.
scenarios.hint: What does +30 mean in -mtime +30, and why preview first?

scenarios.title: Watching the log live
scenarios.situation: You're debugging a live issue and want to watch app.log grow in real time, jumping to the end and searching backwards when something interesting appears.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool and keys?
choices: less +F (follow mode, Ctrl+C to drop to navigation, / to search, q to quit) or tail -f for pure following
cat app.log — it updates live automatically
vim app.log — it reloads on change
head -f — follows the file
scenarios.why: tail -f streams new lines (tail -F survives rotation). less +F gives follow mode PLUS full navigation: Ctrl+C drops back to pager, /pattern searches, n/N jump matches, G goes to end, q quits. For huge files, less never loads the whole file — unlike editors. 'journalctl -f' is the systemd equivalent.
scenarios.hint: Which pager can both follow a growing file and search backwards?

scenarios.title: ifconfig not found
scenarios.situation: A tutorial says to run 'ifconfig' to see your IP. Your system replies 'command not found'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the modern replacement, and what does it show?
choices: 'ip addr' (or 'ip a') — shows interfaces, IPs, and state; ifconfig is deprecated net-tools
ifconfig is required — install it, there's no replacement
cat /etc/hosts — shows your IP
ping localhost — displays interface addresses
scenarios.why: The iproute2 suite ('ip addr', 'ip route', 'ip link') replaced net-tools (ifconfig, route) years ago. 'ip addr' shows each interface's state (UP/DOWN), MAC, IPv4/IPv6 addresses with prefix lengths, and the loopback (lo, 127.0.0.1). Learn iproute2 — ifconfig may not exist on modern minimal systems.
scenarios.hint: Which command family replaced the deprecated net-tools?

scenarios.title: The site won't resolve
scenarios.situation: You can ping 8.8.8.8 but 'ping example.com' fails with 'Name or service not known'.
scenarios.prompt: What does this isolate, and how do you investigate?
choices: IP works but DNS fails — check /etc/resolv.conf nameservers, then test with 'getent hosts example.com' or 'dig example.com'
The network is down — IP ping must have been a fluke
example.com is offline — nothing to investigate
Reboot — DNS fixes itself
scenarios.why: Reaching 8.8.8.8 proves L3 connectivity; name failure isolates DNS. /etc/resolv.conf lists nameservers (often managed by NetworkManager/systemd-resolved — check 'resolvectl status'). 'getent hosts' tests the full NSS path; 'dig'/'host'/'nslookup' query DNS directly. Also check /etc/nsswitch.conf hosts line and /etc/hosts overrides.
scenarios.hint: What works (IP) vs what fails (name) — which layer is broken?

scenarios.title: What's listening?
scenarios.situation: You need to confirm the web server listens on port 80 and see which process owns it.
scenarios.prompt: Which command answers both?
choices: ss -tulpn — TCP/UDP listening sockets with process names (needs root for all processes)
netstat -tulpn — the modern tool
ps aux | grep 80 — processes don't show ports
ls /proc/net/tcp — human-friendly output
scenarios.why: ss (iproute2) replaced netstat: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening, -p process, -n numeric (no DNS lookups — faster). 'ss -tulpn | grep :80' is the standard check. -p needs privileges to see others' processes. Know the well-known ports: 22 SSH, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 53 DNS, 25 SMTP, 3306 MySQL, 5432 Postgres.
scenarios.hint: Which flags mean TCP, listening, process, numeric?

scenarios.title: Copying the backup off the server
scenarios.situation: You need /var/backups/db.sql from server 'db1' to your laptop's current directory, over SSH as user 'ana'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the exact scp syntax?
choices: scp ana@db1:/var/backups/db.sql . — [user@]host:path, '.' is the local destination
scp /var/backups/db.sql db1 — scp guesses the user and direction
ssh db1 cp /var/backups/db.sql . — ssh copies files
scp db1:/var/backups/db.sql — the user is optional and defaults correctly always
scenarios.why: scp source destination with remote form [user@]host:/path. Direction matters: 'scp remote local' downloads, 'scp local remote' uploads. -r recurses directories, -P sets the port (capital P for scp). Modern alternative: 'sftp' or rsync over SSH. First connection prompts to verify the host key — check the fingerprint out-of-band.
scenarios.hint: Which side is the source and which is the destination in the command?

scenarios.title: Fetching the installer
scenarios.situation: Install docs say 'curl -fsSL https://example.com/install.sh | bash'. Your security-conscious teammate objects.
scenarios.prompt: What do the curl flags do, and what is the safer workflow?
choices: -f fail on HTTP errors, -s silent, -S show errors, -L follow redirects — safer: download to a file, inspect it, then run it deliberately
The flags are decorative — piping to bash is always safe
Use wget instead — it's inherently safer than curl
Never install software — the objection means stop entirely
scenarios.why: curl -fsSL is the standard safe-fetch combo (fail loudly on 404s instead of piping an error page to bash, follow redirects). But piping curl to bash executes remote code sight-unseen — download first ('curl -fsSLO ...'), read the script, verify checksums/signatures if provided, then run. wget -qO- is the equivalent fetcher. Convenience vs auditability is the real trade-off.
scenarios.hint: What could go wrong between 'download' and 'execute' if they're the same step?

scenarios.title: Testing before DNS propagates
scenarios.situation: The new site 'shop.example.com' points to 10.0.9.5 internally, but public DNS still shows the old IP. You need to test the new server from your laptop now.
scenarios.prompt: How do you override resolution locally?
choices: Add '10.0.9.5 shop.example.com' to /etc/hosts — it takes precedence over DNS for that name
Edit /etc/resolv.conf — that maps names to IPs
Wait for propagation — local overrides are impossible
/etc/hosts is only for localhost — it can't hold other names
scenarios.why: /etc/hosts provides static name→IP mappings consulted before DNS (per /etc/nsswitch.conf 'hosts: files dns'). It's the standard pre-propagation testing tool and for lab environments. Remember to remove the entry after testing — stale hosts entries cause legendary 'works on my machine' bugs months later.
scenarios.hint: Which file maps names to IPs before DNS is even asked?

Open source licensing: the FSF defines free software by four freedoms: to run, study (requires source), redistribute, and modify/improve (requires source).

Four freedoms: without source, freedoms 1 and 3 are impossible, so it is not free software by this definition.

lessons.title: Finding Your Way — Core concepts
concepts: Paths starting with / are absolute (from root); anything else is relative to the current working directory, so 'home/ana/docs' meant /home/ana/projects/home/ana/docs. Ctrl+R incrementally searches history as you type; '!n' re-executes history entry n; '!!' repeats the last command; tab completes paths.

ls: the first character of ls -l output is the file type: d directory, - regular file, l symlink, plus c/b device files, p pipes, s sockets. 'whereis' also shows binary, source, and man locations. find / works but is slow and shows files PATH would never execute.
Directory purposes: '..' means the parent directory, so '../docs' goes up one then into docs.

example.code:
drwxr-xr-x  4 ana ana 4096 Oct  3 09:12 projects
-rw-r--r--  1 ana ana  220 Oct  3 09:12 notes.txt
lrwxrwxrwx  1 ana ana    8 Oct  3 09:12 latest -> notes.txt
example.walkthrough: The first character of ls -l output is the file type: d directory, - regular file, l symlink, plus c/b device files, p pipes, s sockets. The 'latest -> notes.txt' arrow confirms the symlink's target. 'ls -la' also shows hidden dotfiles.

pitfalls: Common trap: configs → /var, logs → /etc, user files → /opt.
Common trap: history shows commands but they can't be edited or rerun.
Common trap: the docs directory doesn't exist.
Common trap: d = disk, - = network file, l = local file.

lessons.title: CLI Power — Core concepts
concepts: stdout vs stderr: every process has two output streams: stdout (fd 1, the results) and stderr (fd 2, the errors). Pipes (|) feed one command's stdout into the next's stdin. find locates the files, ls -lh gives human sizes, sort -k5 -hr sorts by the size column human-numerically in reverse, head -5 takes the top.
Command composition: glob expansion happens in the shell before the command executes: 'rm * .bak' became 'rm <every file> .bak'.
Command chaining: the command never sees the '*'.
Exit codes are the whole mechanism — 'echo $?' inspects the last one.

lessons.title: Files & Ownership — Core concepts
concepts: Octal notation: the sticky bit (1 in the leading octal digit, shown as t on the execute bit) on a world-writable directory restricts deletion to file owners. /tmp is classically 1777. Each octal digit = one permission triple, summing read(4)+write(2)+execute(1): 7=4+2+1 (rwx), 5=4+1 (r-x), 4=4 (r--).
chown: only root can change file ownership (chown), while owners can change group to groups they belong to (chgrp).
Umask masks OUT permission bits from the defaults (666 files, 777 dirs): subtract (bitwise) the mask.

grep: piping to a second grep -v filters noise. Escalation ladder: TERM → wait → KILL. pkill/killall target by name; 'ps aux' or 'pgrep' finds PIDs.

lessons.title: Linux Essentials — Core concepts
concepts: Everything is a file: devices, processes under /proc, and configuration all appear in the filesystem hierarchy. /etc holds config, /var/log holds logs, /home holds users, /tmp holds scratch.
Permissions are three triples — user, group, other crossed with read, write, execute. chmod 755 means rwxr-xr-x. Directories need the execute bit to enter; files need the read bit to view.
Ownership decides: chown sets user and group; root owns system files. Running as root casually is how systems get broken — use sudo for single commands instead.
Processes have lifecycles: ps lists them, kill sends signals (SIGTERM 15 is the polite default; SIGKILL 9 is the last resort), and jobs plus & manage background work in the shell.

Package managers are per-distro: apt on Debian/Ubuntu, dnf/yum on RHEL/Fedora, pacman on Arch. Always update the index before installing, and prefer signed distro packages over random install scripts.
The shell composes tools: pipes (|) chain commands, redirection (>, >>, 2>) controls output streams, and man pages document everything — man is the fastest senior engineer you will ever meet.

example.code:
ls -l script.sh
chmod 755 script.sh
./script.sh > output.log 2> errors.log
example.walkthrough: ls -l shows the permission triples; chmod 755 adds execute for everyone while keeping write for the owner; the run redirects normal output and errors to separate logs for later review.

pitfalls: Common trap: chmod 777 to 'fix' a permission error — it fixes access by removing all security; find the right user or group instead.
Common trap: kill -9 as the first resort — SIGKILL denies the process any cleanup; try SIGTERM first.
Common trap: piping curl output straight into bash without reading it — prefer signed distro packages.
Common trap: rm -rf with a variable that might be empty — quote it and validate, or an empty variable turns the path into a disaster.

lessons.title: Linux & Cloud Essentials — Core concepts
concepts: Linux follows the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard: configs in /etc, binaries in /usr/bin and /usr/sbin, logs in /var/log, user data in /home — learn the layout once and every system is navigable.
Permissions are user/group/other plus rwx, expressed as octal (755, 640): know how to read them, and use special bits like setgid (2770) for shared directories.
systemd manages services and their logs: 'systemctl status' shows state, 'journalctl -u' shows what the service said — always read logs before restarting blindly.
Cloud computing is rented, metered capacity: you pay for what exists, so idle resources cost money — rightsizing, scheduling, and billing alerts are core cloud skills, not afterthoughts.
Security fundamentals are mostly hygiene: SSH keys instead of shared passwords, least-privilege permissions, updates applied promptly, and firewall defaults that deny.
DevOps is culture plus automation: shared ownership, small frequent releases, blameless learning from incidents — tools serve the practices, not the other way around.

example.code:
ls -l /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo grep -i passwordauth /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sudo systemctl status sshd
example.walkthrough: List the SSH daemon config to confirm it exists and is readable, check whether password authentication is enabled, and verify the service is running. Three commands that answer: does the config exist, what does it say, is the service up.

pitfalls: Common trap: chmod 777 to 'fix' a permission problem — it fixes access by removing all security; find the right user/group/mode instead.
Common trap: restarting a failed service without reading journalctl — you lose the evidence of why it failed.
Common trap: leaving cloud dev resources running 24/7 — schedule them off; the meter never stops on its own.
Common trap: thinking DevOps is a tool purchase — rename the team all you want; practices are the change.

simulations.brief: A script fails with 'No such file or directory' but the file clearly exists when you ls. The path in the script is relative.
simulations.debrief: Relative paths resolve from the working directory, not from the script's location. The fix: use absolute paths or cd to the right directory first — and pwd to confirm where you are.

evidence: $ ./backup.sh -> data/input.csv: No such file or directory
steps.explain: The file exists relative to the script's directory, but the script was run from elsewhere — the relative path resolved against the wrong working directory. Run pwd, cd correctly, or use absolute paths.
options: Check the working directory with pwd and run from the right place (or use absolute paths)

simulations.brief: This backup script is headed for a cron job. Click the problematic lines (2 issues to find).
simulations.debrief: Two scripting mistakes: a relative path (cron runs with a minimal working directory — the path will break), and no error handling (failures go silently unnoticed). Absolute paths and set -euo pipefail are cron-script basics.

steps.config:
#!/bin/bash
cp data/input.csv backups/
echo "backup done"
# runs nightly via cron

issues.description: Relative paths break under cron, which runs with a different working directory.
No error handling — a failed cp still prints 'backup done'.
issues.fix: Add set -euo pipefail at the top.

items: Linux distributions — junior admin work is the direct application of Linux Essentials skills (users, permissions, services, patching).
Open source licensing — the FSF defines free software by four freedoms: to run, study (requires source), redistribute, and modify/improve (requires source).
Copyleft vs permissive — the GPL is a copyleft license: anyone who distributes a modified version must license the whole work under the GPL and provide source.

LTS — LTS releases freeze the software versions and backport security fixes for many years, giving stability and predictability — exactly what unattended kiosks need. Rolling releases change continuously, which risks breaking a locked-down kiosk setup.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
